 What Arkansans said on the first day of early voting for the midterm election
 By 
 Ainsley Platt , Tess Vrbin and Angie Ramirez 
 - 
 October 19, 2026 2:04 pm 
 Voters cast their ballots on the first day of early voting at the Hillary Rodham Clinton Children’s Library in Little Rock, Arkansas on Monday, Oct. 19, 2026. (Photo by Ainsley Platt/Arkansas Advocate)
 Polls across Arkansas opened for early voting Monday, with thousands of people expected to cast their ballots before Election Day next month. 
 Poll times 
 Polls will be open from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. Monday through Friday until Election Day, and from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. Saturdays. Polls will close at 5 p.m. the day before the election. 
 Voters will decide whether to grant Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders , U.S. Sen. Tom Cotton and the state’s four congressmen — all Republicans — new terms. All six are facing Democratic challengers, and some are also contending with Libertarian candidates. 
 Samantha Boyd, a spokesperson for the Arkansas secretary of state’s office, said it anticipated 500,000 people, or half of the total number of people expected to cast a ballot, to vote early this year. 
 Here’s what Arkansans said about the candidates and the issues as they early voted: 
 Republican voters cite Trump ties as a plus
 Saline County, a Republican stronghold in central Arkansas, saw nearly 600 voters by mid-morning Monday, county communications director Trevor Villines said. 
 Some voters expressed enthusiasm for Republican candidates such as Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders. 
 “She’s in there doing the job right, and we need somebody that’s going to continue doing the job right,” said AJ Burchfield of Haskell, who voted Republican in every state and federal race. 
 William Good was among the Arkansans who voted early at the Saline County courthouse on Monday, Oct. 19, 2026. (Photo by Tess Vrbin/Arkansas Advocate) 
 Retired police officer William Good of Benton said voting Republican down the ballot mattered most to him. He said he hadn’t read the ballot measures and that he wanted to vote for anyone aligned with President Donald Trump, including U.S. Sen. Tom Cotton and U.S. Rep. French Hill. 
 Democrats cite frustration with president 
 Other Benton residents said their frustrations with the Trump administration motivated them to vote for Democrats, including Hill’s opponent, Chris Jones, and Cotton’s opponent Hallie Shoffner. 
 “[I hope] we are sending candidates to Congress that are going to help balance the scales rather than support blindly those who are already in power,” said Tanner Oglesby, a teacher. 
 Robert Zimmerman said he typically votes for Democrats because Republicans “represent everything that’s wrong in this country,” such as cuts to public benefits and Social Security . 
 Neil McElhaney said he also supported Shoffner and Jones because “it’s time for a change.” He said elected Republicans’ rhetoric toward immigrants and LGBTQ+ people frustrates him. 
 Tanner Oglesby, voter in Saline County, on the first day of early voting in Arkansas on Monday, Oct. 19, 2026 (Photo by Tess Vrbin/Arkansas Advocate) 
 On the local level, Oglesby and McElhaney said they voted against Saline County’s proposal to reduce the property tax funding the local library system. 
 “We need to keep the library funded,” McElhaney said. “Education is key. My mother, being a retired English teacher, has always stressed education.” 
 Pulaski County voter opposing incumbents 
 Pulaski County’s downtown Little Rock polling site saw a steady stream of voters Monday morning, with several people standing outside waving signs mainly for Democratic candidates, though some were holding signs for Libertarians and Republicans too. 
 Voters who spoke with the Arkansas Advocate indicated their votes were to oppose incumbents such as Cotton and Hill. 
 Sarah King of Little Rock said she voted for Shoffner and Jones because she believed they have morals that their opponents do not. 
 “I just think we have an administration right now that is not kind, is not worried about human rights,” King said. 
 She said she was opposed to Flock cameras that have popped up all over the state, and was particularly concerned about how immigrants have been treated under the Trump administration. 
 Democratic congressional nominee Chris Jones voting with his daughters Janelle (13, left) and Jasmine (10, right) at the Pulaski County early voting site in downtown Little Rock on Monday, Oct. 19, 2026. Jones is running against Republican U.S. Rep. French Hill in the 2nd Congressional District (Photo by Tess Vrbin/Arkansas Advocate) 
 “These are my neighbors and this is my community,” King said. “I have a son, and I want him to know also that I didn’t support this.” 
 Retired teacher says accountability a concern 
 Faye Hanson, a retired teacher from North Little Rock who has traditionally supported Democrats, said her biggest concern while researching candidates was accountability. She said Cotton and Hill don’t meet enough with their constituents. 
 “They’re not doing the work for us, and they’re getting paid a lot of money and have great healthcare and they’re voting against our interests,” Hanson said. “I think a lot of our public servants at all levels have forgotten who they work for.” 
 Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Hallie Shoffner casts her ballot at the Hillary Rodham Clinton Children’s Library in Little Rock on the first day of early voting on Monday, Oct. 19, 2026 (Photo by Ainsley Platt/Arkansas Advocate) 
 Hanson also said she opposed all four ballot measures Arkansans will decide on. The lack of a process for creating the economic development districts proposed in Issue 3 were concerning for her because she doesn’t “trust the people in power right now to use our money wisely.” She said she couldn’t support Issue 4 either, which would allow the state to issue up to half a billion dollars worth of bonds for water and wastewater infrastructure. 
 Jessica Roberts declined to say who she voted for, but said in general that the people already in office at all levels — local, state and federal — weren’t following through on the promises they made on the campaign trail. Roberts cited gun violence as a concern in the area. 
 “Some people that we already have in there, they say that they are gonna do this for the kids and do that for the kids, and we don’t see none of that,” Roberts said.  
 Northwest Arkansas voter says Congress needs to check president’s power
 Bruce Wilkinson, a Benton County voter, said he went to the polls early alongside his wife because he wanted to make his voice heard.
 Campaign signs line the sidewalk near the Benton County Election Commission in Rogers, Arkansas on the first day of early voting on Monday, Oct. 19, 2026. (Photo by Angie Ramirez/Arkansas Advocate) 
 “We wanted to get the earliest in,” Wilkinson said. “We were anxious to do it early.”
 Wilkinson said that members of the House and Senate had failed to fulfill their responsibility to check presidential power.
 “The issue is the fact that Congress let the president do whatever he wanted and not properly check him.” Wilkinson said.
 Wilkinson said he hoped voters would replace officials who had not carried out their constitutional role. For him, the election is an opportunity to change who represents the public and to hold elected officials accountable.
 Although Wilkinson was glad to have cast his ballot, he said the election is not finished until the results are announced and every vote is counted.
 “I’ll feel better on Nov. 3 when we get the results, and everything is finally counted,” he said.
 Local race the biggest draw for a Rogers voter
 June Galloway stood outside Benton County Election Commission as a nonpartisan voter supporting Mallory Sanders in her campaign for Rogers City Council.  
 Galloway said Sanders’ experience as an attorney and a teacher at Northwest Arkansas Community College distinguished her from the other candidates in the race.   Galloway emphasized that her support was not based on party affiliation.  
 “I’m not here as a Democrat or Republican,” Galloway said. “I’m here as a nonpartisan to support Mallory.”  
 Signs for several candidates line the street outside the Pulaski County Regional Building in Little Rock, Arkansas on the first day of early voting on Monday, Oct. 19, 2026 (Photo by Tess Vrbin/Arkansas Advocate)

 Author Info
 Ainsley Platt
 Ainsley covers the environment, energy and other topics as a reporter for the Arkansas Advocate. Ainsley came to the Advocate after nearly two years at the Arkansas Democrat-Gazette, where she covered energy and environment, and Arkansas' nascent lithium industry. She has earned accolades for her use of FOIA in her reporting at the ADG, and for her stories about discrimination and student government as a staff reporter, and later as the news desk editor, for The Crimson White, The University of Alabama's student newspaper.
 Arkansas Advocate is part of States Newsroom , the nation’s largest state-focused nonprofit news organization.
 MORE FROM AUTHOR Tess Vrbin
 Tess Vrbin came to the Advocate from the Arkansas Democrat-Gazette, where she reported on low-income housing and tenants' rights, and won awards for her coverage of 2021 flooding and tornado damage in rural Arkansas. She previously covered local government for The Commercial Dispatch in Mississippi and state government for the Columbia Daily Tribune in Missouri.
 Arkansas Advocate is part of States Newsroom , the nation’s largest state-focused nonprofit news organization.
 MORE FROM AUTHOR Angie Ramirez
 Angie Ramirez is a journalism student at the University of Arkansas, where she serves as assistant editor for Hill Magazine and president of the campus chapter of the National Association of Hispanic Journalists. She began her journalism training at the U of A as a participant in the Lemke Journalism Project during her last two years of high school and now serves as a coordinator for the program.
